idiom_name: rust_decimal::Decimal in a Money<C> newtype with a currency marker
implementation_notes: Rust has no decimal primitive and no currency type in core, so the pattern splits into representation plus typing: rust_decimal supplies a 128-bit fixed-precision decimal (96-bit mantissa plus scale, roughly 28 significant digits) with round_dp, RoundingStrategy, serde support and a dec! macro, while a Money newtype pairs it with a currency marker - a type parameter or a Currency enum - so the compiler refuses to add USD to EUR. Both this and the integer route replace the classic class with a Copy value type plus impl Add/Sub/Mul and a checked or Result-returning API on overflow; serialization must emit a string or minor-unit integer, because JSON has no decimal type.
pitfalls: Rounding is not automatic: without round_dp after every length-changing operation, scales and trailing zeros leak into comparisons and serialization.
Decimal tops out near 28 significant digits, so compounding interest silently loses precision past that.
The currency marker is phantom, so deserialization must validate the code rather than trust the type parameter.
Integer arithmetic wraps in release builds and Decimal operations can overflow, which is why the checked API exists and should be used for totals.

variants.name: Int64 minor units in a no_std value type
variants.idiom_name: Money<C>(i64, PhantomData<C>) with the exponent in the currency type
variants.implementation_notes: Where no_std, determinism or throughput dominate, store i64 minor units and carry the exponent as an associated constant of the currency type, so arithmetic is integer-only and allocation-free. Percentages and division then go through helpers that multiply in i128 and round once, and allocation is explicit (largest remainder); this is the fixed-scale counterpart of the decimal route and the one to choose for clearing and ledger hot paths.
pitfalls: i64 overflow wraps in release builds, so totals need checked_add or i128 intermediates.
Rates and percentages must be expressed as integers (basis points) or floats sneak back into the arithmetic.
Runtime-parsed currency codes cannot become type parameters, so a validated enum or a runtime check is still required.
